description:
The Galleria Dorata — the Golden Gallery — is the visual centrepiece of Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino and the single most spectacular room among the four palaces on the Rolli guided tour. Added by the Carrega family in 1704, a full century and a half after the original palace was completed, it covers every surface — walls, vaulted ceiling, furnishings, and mirrors — in gilded stucco, carved wood, and frescoes by Lorenzo De Ferrari, the leading Genoese painter of the early 18th century. The Galleria Dorata is a textbook example of how a Renaissance palace becomes a Rococo palace without demolishing its structure: the Carrega family did not rebuild Giovanni Battista Castello's original shell; they layered an interior that expressed their own period's taste with unrestrained confidence across a late-Renaissance building, giving the palace two distinct architectural identities that coexist today.

The palace's four chapters of ownership are embedded in its names. Built in 1558–1561 for Tobia Pallavicino — making it the earliest of the three Bergamasco-designed palaces on Via Garibaldi — it passed to the Carrega family in 1704, who commissioned the Golden Gallery and gave the building its architectural signature. The Cataldi barons acquired it in 1830, and the composite name Palazzo Carrega-Cataldi has persisted since; it is the name used by the Genoa Chamber of Commerce, which purchased the building in 1922. That institutional acquisition was consequential: Chamber of Commerce ownership prevented the palace from being subdivided, funded successive restoration campaigns, and is the direct reason the building stands intact and accessible to visitors through the Rolli guided tour today.

The original 16th-century decorative programme is most legible in the vestibules — the ground-floor and main-floor entrance spaces where Bergamasco's late-Renaissance stucco in grotesque ornament and painted panels survive largely intact beneath the Rococo overlay. First-time visitors often move through these rooms quickly on the way to the Galleria Dorata; returning attention to them rewards the effort, since they represent the palace's founding aesthetic before the Carrega transformation and demonstrate the specific decorative vocabulary that Bergamasco deployed across all three of his Via Garibaldi commissions.

Access to Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino is through the guided Rolli Palaces tour, a 2.5-hour bilingual Italian/English circuit covering all four Via Garibaldi Rolli palaces. The guide's commentary in the Galleria Dorata — explaining the De Ferrari fresco programme, the specific Rococo ornamental vocabulary, and the logic of the Carrega family's transformation of a Bergamasco shell — is the key that makes the room fully legible to first-time visitors.
history: Via Garibaldi took shape in the 1550s as Genoa's most ambitious planned residential street. Tobia Pallavicino was among the first to build on it, commissioning Giovanni Battista Castello — "il Bergamasco" — to design a late-Renaissance palace completed by 1561, the earliest of the Bergamasco trio on the street. The building's original stucco vestibules decorated with grotesque ornament established the architectural vocabulary Bergamasco would develop across two further Via Garibaldi commissions within the decade. For more than a century the palace served within the Rolli system — one of the noble residences placed by Senate decree at the disposal of visiting state dignitaries. In 1704 the Carrega family acquired the property and commissioned Lorenzo De Ferrari to add the Galleria Dorata: a Rococo showpiece covering every surface in gilded stucco, carved wood, and fresco. The Cataldi barons purchased the palace in 1830, lending it the composite name Palazzo Carrega-Cataldi still used today. The Genoa Chamber of Commerce acquired the building in 1922, keeping it undivided and funding the restoration campaigns that preserved its architectural fabric through the following century. The palace entered the UNESCO World Heritage System in 2006 as part of the Rolli inscription.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino is at Via Garibaldi 4, at the lower end of the street as you approach from Piazza Fontane Marose — the first of the four palaces you'd encounter walking up Via Garibaldi from the eastern entrance. The nearest metro station is De Ferrari (~5 minutes' walk). The guided tour starting point will be confirmed when booking.

**Tickets:** Access is via the guided Rolli Palaces tour (t29705, from €15, 4.5★ / 593 reviews) — a 2.5-hour bilingual Italian/English tour including Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino alongside Palazzo Imperiale, Palazzo Rosso, and Palazzo Lomellino. The Golden Gallery is the centrepiece of this stop; confirm it is included in the tour's current itinerary when booking.

**Practical tips:** The Golden Gallery is easy to underestimate from the exterior — the palace's street facade is relatively understated. Insist on seeing the Galleria Dorata specifically, and take time inside it. The stucco vestibules on the ground and main floors are also impressive once you know to look for them — the original Renaissance decoration programme under the Rococo overlay. The tour's bilingual Italian/English format covers all four palaces; the guide's commentary in the Galleria Dorata is particularly valuable for understanding the De Ferrari frescoes.

**Combine with:** [Palazzo Lomellino](/castles/italy/palazzo-lomellino) (one of the three Bergamasco-designed palaces on the same tour — the Strozzi-frescoed palace with coral-trade origins and the only Rolli palace with hanging gardens) and [Palazzo Imperiale](/castles/italy/palazzo-imperiale) (the third of the Bergamasco trio, still owned by the Imperiale family for which it was built in c.1560).

faqs.question: Why does this palace have two names?
faqs.answer: Built for Tobia Pallavicino in 1558, the palace was acquired by the Carrega family in 1704 — who added the Galleria Dorata — and then by the Cataldi barons in 1830, who added their name alongside the Carrega's. The resulting composite Palazzo Carrega-Cataldi is the name the Genoa Chamber of Commerce (owners since 1922) continues to use today. On the GetYourGuide Rolli tour, the palace is listed under its original founding name, Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino.

faqs.question: What is the Golden Gallery?
faqs.answer: The Galleria Dorata, added by the Carrega family in 1704, is a Rococo showpiece room where every surface — walls, vaulted ceiling, furnishings, and mirrors — is covered in gilded stucco, carved wood, and frescoes by Lorenzo De Ferrari, the leading Genoese painter of the early 18th century. It is the visual highlight of the four Rolli palaces on the guided tour, and a precise example of the transformation from Renaissance shell to Rococo interior that characterised aristocratic patronage in 18th-century Genoa.

faqs.question: Who owns Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino today?
faqs.answer: The Genoa Chamber of Commerce, which purchased the building in 1922. Chamber of Commerce ownership has kept the palace in continuous institutional use, preventing subdivision and funding the restoration campaigns that have preserved its architectural fabric — including both the original Bergamasco stucco vestibules and the 18th-century Galleria Dorata. The Rolli guided tour provides public access to the palace's interiors.

faqs.question: Who designed it and who else did that architect work for?
faqs.answer: Giovanni Battista Castello, known as "il Bergamasco," designed Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino in 1558–1561 — his earliest known commission on Via Garibaldi. He went on to design Palazzo Imperiale (c. 1560) and Palazzo Lomellino (1563–1569) on the same street, creating an unusually concentrated body of work: three late-Renaissance palaces by a single architect, at the same scale, within about a decade, on what became the most architecturally consistent Renaissance street in Italy.
